newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN WHEAT FARMERS URGED TO DIVERSIFY CROPS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN WHEAT FARMERS URGED TO DIVERSIFY CROPS.

text.p: The deregulation of South Africa's wheat industry would lead to a greater emphasis on quality, forcing some farmers to diversify into other crops.

In an article in the latest issue of the University of Cape Town's Trade Monitor, economics lecturer Lawrence Edwards said farmers in the Western Cape, who produced low quality wheat, would be particularly vulnerable.
"Farmers must adjust their production options through increased diversification to limit their risk exposure to a single commodity," Edwards said.
They should also concentrate more on improving the quality of wheat produced through better management and the use of better wheat cultivars.
He said the Western Cape, which produces 31 percent of South African wheat would face a quality price differential with wheat produced in the Free State.
This would be exacerbated by the fact that the Western Cape was further away from the prime milling area of Gauteng province and would have to face the full brunt of international prices.
Legislation passed late last year abolishes single channel marketing of agricultural products but gives statutory control boards a 13-month window period to reshape themselves.
The Wheat Board will retain its 50-year-old one-channel marketing system, as well as its sole right to import or export wheat, until the end of the 1996/97 season on October 31.

As European and American wheat farmers received some form of subsidy from their governments, local farmers might need compensatory protection through tariffs to enable them to compete internationally, Edwards said.
"Although these suggestions are not appropriate at present given high international wheat prices and a depreciating rand, this favourable context may be shortlived," Edwards said.
He said farmers must use the period until deregulation to re-establish marketing links such as procurement, pricing, storage and grading that were previously performed through the Wheat Board.
